# Websites, Search, and Sharing

## 1. Scope

Project websites are public product surfaces. They must explain the project clearly to people, search engines, and other systems that read or share their content.

These standards apply to every official website and public web documentation of a Plystra project, whatever the medium of the underlying work. They do not require private application content to become public or indexable.

## 2. Honest, useful content

Search visibility must come from content that accurately explains the project.

Public pages must:

- say what the project does and who it serves;
- distinguish current capabilities from planned work;
- state maturity and limitations when needed to understand the offer;
- describe ownership, publishing, and sponsorship relationships with the [relationship wording](https://github.com/plystra/craft/blob/main/principles/01-brand-philosophy.md#5-brand-hierarchy-and-relationship-wording);
- keep metadata and machine-readable summaries consistent with visible content.

Public sites carry no roadmap, milestone list, or gate status. One plain line about maturity is enough; plans belong in the project's own documentation, not on its public pages.

Do not use keyword stuffing, misleading previews, invented reviews, or unsupported claims to attract traffic. Search and sharing copy follows the same [writing standards](https://github.com/plystra/craft/blob/main/principles/03-language-and-writing.md) as the product.

## 3. Readable pages and navigation

The initial HTML response for pages intended for indexing must contain their primary content, meaningful links, and page metadata. Visitors and crawlers must not need to complete an animation, interact with a control, or run application code to discover the page's purpose.

Use semantic headings and descriptive links. Important public pages must be reachable through ordinary links, not only search boxes or scripted navigation.

Static generation and server rendering are both suitable approaches. Choose the simplest rendering strategy that satisfies these requirements and the project's maintenance needs.

Set the document language correctly. When actual translated versions exist, use consistent language metadata and appropriate alternate-language links; do not advertise translations that do not exist.

## 4. Page identity and canonical URLs

Every indexable page must provide:

- a specific title that identifies the page and project;
- an accurate description that helps a reader decide whether the page is relevant;
- an absolute canonical URL on the intended public HTTPS origin;
- a stable address that can be opened directly and shared.

Distinct pages must have appropriately distinct titles and descriptions. Keep them concise and place useful information early. Character counts are editorial guidance, not guarantees that search engines will display the text unchanged or in full.

Canonical URLs, internal links, sharing metadata, structured data, and sitemap entries must agree about the intended URL. Document conventions for trailing slashes and other equivalent URL forms, and redirect obsolete addresses when a replacement exists.

Prefer shared metadata helpers or a common content source to prevent drift. The implementation must still allow page-specific text and URLs.

## 5. Crawling and indexing

Every official website must publish a deliberate `robots.txt` policy and a valid `sitemap.xml` at its public origin. The robots file must identify the sitemap with an absolute URL.

The sitemap must contain only canonical public URLs intended for indexing that return successful page responses. Exclude:

- error pages, including `404` pages;
- redirects and duplicate URL variants;
- pages marked `noindex`;
- private, authenticated, preview, and internal pages.

Keep the sitemap synchronized with the published pages. Generating it from the site's authoritative page inventory is recommended. Use `lastmod` only when reliable content modification dates exist; a routine build is not evidence that every page changed.

Use page-level robots metadata or an appropriate HTTP header when a publicly reachable page must not be indexed. A crawler needs access to read `noindex`; do not rely on a crawl prohibition to convey it.

`robots.txt`, canonical links, and `noindex` are not access controls. Protect private content through authentication and authorization. Preview deployments must also have an intentional access and indexing policy.

Missing pages must return an appropriate error status. Do not serve a successful empty shell or the home page for every unknown URL.

## 6. Sharing previews and site identity

Public pages must provide Open Graph metadata with an accurate title, description, canonical page URL, site identity, appropriate content type, and share image. Provide compatible Twitter card metadata with an explicit card type. Include the image's absolute HTTPS URL and alternative text, and declare its dimensions in Open Graph metadata.

Language and locale metadata must reflect the page's content. A large-image card is recommended when the image supports the preview well.

Share images must be publicly fetchable without authentication, legible at preview size, and consistent with the page's claims and visual identity. A site-wide image is acceptable when it accurately represents the page; use a specific image when the content needs one.

A landscape image around `1200 × 630` is a useful default, subject to the requirements of the sharing surfaces the project supports. Use a compatible image format and check actual cropping and text readability.

Keep the source or a reproducible creation process for share images with the website's maintained assets. Update previews when the project's name, positioning, or status changes.

Provide a recognizable favicon with a broadly supported fallback. Touch icons and browser theme colors are recommended where they improve presentation on supported devices.

## 7. Structured data

Use JSON-LD for applicable website and project entities. Choose vocabulary that matches the actual content and project type; do not label every project as the same kind of software.

Structured data must:

- describe facts supported by the visible site;
- use stable identifiers and canonical URLs;
- identify the real publisher or responsible organization;
- distinguish ownership from sponsorship;
- link to source repositories or other resources only when they exist and are public;
- reflect the actual release or development state.

Do not invent ratings, availability, affiliations, or legal status. Validate the syntax and the relevant vocabulary. Valid structured data does not guarantee a search feature or enhanced result.

## 8. Machine-readable website summary

Every official website must publish a publicly accessible `/llms.txt` in plain text or Markdown, kept with the site's maintained content.

It must contain:

- the project name and a concise factual description;
- the current maturity or maintenance status;
- canonical links to the official website and relevant public documentation;
- links to public source repositories when available;
- any limitations needed to avoid presenting planned work as available behavior.

The summary must agree with the public website and exclude private infrastructure details, credentials, unpublished material, and misleading instructions to automated readers.

`llms.txt` complements readable HTML, metadata, `robots.txt`, and the sitemap. It does not replace them, control access, or guarantee that any system will read, index, or rank the site.

## 9. Performance and accessibility

Search preparation must preserve the site's [accessibility standards](https://github.com/plystra/craft/blob/main/principles/06-accessibility-and-interaction.md) and usable performance.

Important text must remain readable throughout supported animation states. Accessible link names must accurately identify the visible destination or action. Sharing images need meaningful alternative text.

Optimize image delivery, font loading, and unnecessary script work according to the page's needs. Preload only resources shown to be important to initial rendering; do not preload every font or image by default.

Automated audit scores are diagnostic evidence. They do not prove accessibility, indexing, ranking, or the quality of the content, and a perfect score is not a substitute for reviewing the page.

## 10. Release verification

Before publishing or materially changing a website, verify the production build and the deployed responses:

1. Primary content, headings, language, titles, descriptions, and canonical URLs are present in the returned HTML.
2. Real pages, redirects, and missing pages return appropriate HTTP status codes.
3. `robots.txt`, `sitemap.xml`, and `/llms.txt` are reachable and agree with the site's public content and indexing policy.
4. The sitemap excludes private, duplicate, redirected, missing, and `noindex` URLs.
5. Share metadata and image URLs resolve correctly, and representative previews are readable.
6. JSON-LD is valid and describes the correct entities and relationships.
7. Key pages remain usable on supported viewports, with reduced motion and assistive technologies considered.

Record the scope and results of checks in the release or review notes. Check actual responses, not only source templates. Use automated audits alongside manual inspection of representative pages and previews.

Recheck these surfaces when routes, domains, project status, ownership, or public descriptions change. Preserve useful redirects and update public summaries when a project is retired.
